name: Rosa Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you actually think. Okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Totally fine. I'm curious about this stuff anyway, so ask away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulldozer at a big lithium mine, an open pit out in dry scrub country. Most of my shift is pushing waste rock, building ramps for the haul trucks and keeping the tip edge safe so nobody drives off it. The dozer has a GPS system that shows me the design levels on a screen, and I'm still learning to read the ground by feel instead of staring at the screen. My trainer, Kofi, says I'm quick with the tech and slow with the blade, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh, that would be a bit of a letdown for me. I use AI tools every day, I like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that AI turned out to be a nice helper, not a takeover. Online I'd post something about the tools I still find useful, because people would be saying it was all useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it changes nothing. I already ask an AI to explain every alarm code on my dozer, and it's still me pushing the dirt. The lithium market is the bigger thing in my life, and prices have been up and down all year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the dozer and aim to be signed off for night work by spring. I'd keep putting money into an index fund each month, I've got about three months of costs saved plus a little in shares. And I'd keep using the AI to study for my next ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bored, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lithium prices are up and down. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Last year they slowed hiring when the price dropped, but nobody got cut. I've got savings and there are other pits nearby, so I'd find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the next ticket you're studying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grader, which smooths the haul roads. I like having two machines on my card, because the more machines you can run, the harder you are to let go.

say: AI turned out to be a **nice helper**, not a takeover.
She'd post online about the **useful tools** others had written off.
think: Nothing changes for her, since the **dozer** still needs her.
**Lithium prices** matter more to her than AI.
do: Get signed off for **night work** on the dozer by spring.
Keep paying monthly into an **index fund**.
Study for a **grader ticket** with AI help.
S0.quote: I already ask an AI to explain every alarm code on my dozer, and it's still me pushing the dirt.
fieldNote: Daily **AI user** who would be mildly disappointed by a plateau.
Her main pressure is **commodity prices**, softened by savings and nearby pits.
She deliberately collects **machine tickets** to be harder to let go.

steps.text: Get signed off for night shifts on the dozer by spring
Keep paying a set amount into an index fund each month
Use an AI tutor to study for the grader ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one sounds about right to me. And it sounds pretty good for lithium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the people who learn the new systems will be fine. I'd probably post about the remote operations centre jobs, because lots of people don't know they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Lithium goes into every car battery, so a slow AI change just means more pits and more seats for people who can run a screen. Dozers on rough ground are one of the last machines to go fully robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the company's remote operations pilot straight away, since they already asked for volunteers. I'd do a short online course in mine automation systems, a few hundred dollars from savings. And I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more in battery-metal shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It feels like the ground's shifting my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, my trainer, is brilliant on the blade but hates screens. I'd want to help him learn the remote stuff, but he'd probably tell me to mind my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put more into battery-metal shares. Isn't that doubling your bet on lithium?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair point. If lithium crashes, I lose the job and the shares together. Maybe I'd keep it to a small slice and put the rest in a general fund.

She'd post about **remote operations** jobs most people don't know exist.

do: Volunteer for the company's **remote operations** pilot straight away.
Pay for a short online **automation course** from savings.
Keep investing, with only a **small slice** in battery-metal shares.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, like the ground is shifting her way.

fieldNote: She reads this picture as an **opportunity**, given lithium demand and her tech comfort.

Her worry goes to her **trainer**, who resists screens.

steps.text: Volunteer for the company's remote operations pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's where it stops being fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say it's too fast and governments need to catch up, with some kind of support for people who lose work. I'd say it calmly, though, because panicking online doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the remote operations job goes first. My plan was to be the person who watches the robots, and in two years the AI watches the robots. Then the dozer itself goes around 2031, so I'd have three years at most in the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the dozer and work every extra shift to build savings, because the hands-on job lasts longer than the screen job. I'd start looking for work that mixes hands and people, maybe training others on the new robots while that lasts. And I'd move most of my shares into cash, because I'd want it ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The thing I was good at, the tech, suddenly isn't special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a job you'd look at outside mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something like firefighting or emergency work. Out here, when the bushfires come, people still need people. But I don't know if that's realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your housemate, who works in the mine office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya to start looking now, because her payroll job goes in 2028, not 2031. She'd be worse off than me, and we split the rent, so that's my problem too.

say: It's **too fast**, and governments need to catch up with support.
She'd say it **calmly**, because online panic helps nobody.
think: The **remote operations** job she aimed for goes first.
She'd have about **three years** in the dozer before robots arrive.
do: Work **extra shifts** in the dozer to build savings.
Look for work **training others** on new robots.
feel: **Anxious**, because her tech skills suddenly aren't special.
S2.quote: My plan was to be the person who watches the robots, and in two years the AI watches the robots.
fieldNote: She understood the **thinking-first** order: her screen plan dies before her dozer job.
Her **housemate's office job** threatens her rent split too.
She floats **emergency work** but doubts it herself.

steps.text: Work every extra dozer shift until 2031 to build savings
Apply for jobs training crews on the new robots
Move most shares into cash savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, 2034 for robots. That's a real window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time if we start now, and I'd try to get people at work to take it seriously. I'd probably organise a lunch session on what's coming, because nobody else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I could get ahead of it. Five years is enough to get one step ahead of the machines, if I start the day I hear about it. I'd aim for something that needs people even after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the dozer job and start a part-time diploma in work health and safety in 2027, because sites with robots still need someone responsible for people. I'd keep investing but more cautiously. And I'd tell Priya to start her own retraining early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a get-on-with-it way. I like having a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why safety, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when something goes wrong on site, someone has to talk to the family, the regulator and the crew. I can't see a robot being trusted with that soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends away. I go camping most days off, and I'd swap half of that for study. It'd hurt, but five years goes fast.

She'd organise a **lunch session** at work about what's coming.
think: She can **get ahead** of the change with five years.
She wants work that **needs people** even after robots arrive.
do: Start a part-time **safety diploma** in 2027 while dozing.
feel: **Uneasy** but energised by having a project.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get one step ahead of the machines, if I start the day I hear about it.
fieldNote: She picks **health and safety** because it centres on human trust and responsibility.
She'd act as an informal **organiser** at work.
She trades **camping weekends** for study, a real personal cost.

steps.text: Start a part-time work health and safety diploma in 2027
Keep investing monthly but in a broad, low-risk fund
Cut camping trips by half to free up study time and money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. I'd be thirty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case of the three AGI ones, and companies should start training people now instead of waiting. I'd keep posting about remote jobs and new tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd use it to move up properly. Ten years of warning is a gift, and I'd hate to be the one who wasted it sitting in a dozer. I could do the safety diploma, then maybe a degree part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the safety diploma by 2029 and then move into a site safety role. I'd keep investing steadily and maybe buy a small unit with a deposit by 2030. I'd still keep my dozer ticket current as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. It feels like a long game I could actually win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in mining at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, at least in the safety side. I like the sites, the people, the scale of it. I just don't want to be the person in the seat when the seat goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the whole town shrinks. If robots run the pit, there are fewer people, fewer shops, fewer friends. I'd have a good job in an empty place.

say: It's the **best case** of the three AGI pictures by far.
Companies should start **training people** now, not wait.
think: She'd use the decade to **move up** properly.
Wasting ten years **sitting in a dozer** would be her failure.
do: Finish a **safety diploma** by 2029 and move into site safety.
Keep her **dozer ticket** current as a backup.
feel: **Uneasy** but optimistic, like a long game she can win.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is a gift, and I'd hate to be the one who wasted it sitting in a dozer.
fieldNote: She treats ten years as a **gift** and feels responsible for using it.
Her lingering worry is a **shrinking town**, not her own job.
She keeps a **backup ticket**, consistent with collecting machine skills.

steps.text: Move into a site safety officer role after qualifying
Buy a small unit with a deposit by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the tech skills I'm proud of stop counting. I'm the one on my crew who reads the update notes on the dozer screen, and even I'm not sure that's enough. What would help is companies paying for retraining into jobs that need people, like safety and training, before the robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the towns. Everyone asks about jobs, but a mining town is a whole life. If the people go, it's not just a job you lose.

headlineQuote: I'm the one on my crew who reads the update notes on the dozer screen, and even I'm not sure that's enough.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old bulldozer** operator at a lithium mine, single and sharing a rented house.
She uses **AI daily**, invests a little each month and collects machine tickets.
In slow pictures she's **calm**, seeing lithium demand and remote jobs as openings.
In **AGI by 2028** her screen plan vanishes first, making her anxious.
With more time she plans a **safety career**, worrying mainly about a shrinking town.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her tech skills stop counting before her dozer job ends.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid retraining** into people-centred jobs like safety and training.
